ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Progress Note 5 — Preventive Visit — Samuel Johnson

code.displayName: Periodic reevaluation and management of healthy individual

text.paragraph: Mr. Johnson is a 55-year-old writer with recurrent major depression on sertraline 100 mg and Tourette syndrome treated with behavioral therapy for tics, who comes for his yearly preventive visit five weeks after his eleven-week review. His mood has kept improving: he writes most mornings, dines with friends several times a week, and his PHQ-9 today is 7. He finished his eight sessions of behavioral therapy for tics last week and uses a competing response for the head-shaking tic when he chooses to. He sleeps from about two until nine. He has no side effects from sertraline apart from mild sweating at night. He has had no preventive care for many years. [S]

Major depressive disorder, recurrent, severe, without psychotic features: low mood, loss of interest, poor sleep, guilt, and withdrawal from company for about three months on a background of depression that never fully lifted after a severe episode last year; first episode at about twenty; synthetic modern episode linked to his documented melancholy
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis by DSM-5 criteria; the record makes no claim about his real mental health.
Motor and vocal tics since childhood, with ritual counting and stepping behaviors, never formally diagnosed; neurology evaluation requested
S — Synthetic presenting concern anchored to the documented tics; superseded by the diagnosis at the neurology consultation.

Tourette syndrome: multiple motor tics and vocal tics since childhood, with premonitory urges, brief suppressibility, and tic-related obsessive-compulsive symptoms (counting, evening-up, and threshold rituals); synthetic modern diagnosis by DSM-5 criteria at the neurology consultation, linked to the documented tics and to the retrospective diagnosis
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis; the retrospective historical diagnosis is graded R and is not asserted as fact.

Blindness of the left eye since early childhood after scrofula (tuberculous cervical lymphadenitis), with old scars of the neck and face; right eye myopic, corrected to normal; synthetic modern coding linked to his documented loss of sight in one eye
S — Synthetic modern coding; the source does not say which eye, so the left is a synthetic choice.

Periodic adult preventive visit completed. Health risk assessment reviewed and the prevention plan updated. Colorectal cancer screening, vaccines, and an eye examination were overdue. 10-year cardiovascular risk estimated at about 6% with LDL 138 mg/dL, below the threshold at which a statin is recommended. [S]
Next preventive visit in one year.

Major depressive disorder, recurrent, improving on sertraline (F33.2). PHQ-9 7, from 21 at intake and 10 five weeks ago. Night sweats are a known, mild sertraline effect. Safety reviewed: no thoughts of suicide or self-harm; the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline is on his safety plan. [S]
Continue sertraline 100 mg daily and psychotherapy.

Blindness of the left eye (H54.42). With sight in one eye only, protecting and checking the right eye matters more than usual. [S]

Guideline basis: VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for Assessment and Management of Patients at Risk for Suicide (2024); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monograph (2026); Medicare Preventive Services reference: visit templates, screening cascades, and documentation elements (2026); USPSTF A and B Recommendations (2026); Adult Immunization Schedule by Medical Condition and Other Indication (2026)

Follow-up: Six-month review in the autumn, with the second zoster and hepatitis B doses and the influenza vaccine. FIT kit to be returned within two weeks; HIV result by letter, as he asked. Eye examination arranged. Next preventive visit in one year. Next scheduled visit 2026-09-28: six-month review of depression and tics. [S]

Voluntary advance care planning discussion of about 18 minutes, with his consent. He named a longtime friend as his health care agent, and a health care proxy form was completed; the agent is recorded in the chart and is not named here. He said that what matters most to him is keeping his mind clear, being told the truth about his condition, and having time to prepare himself in prayer if he becomes seriously ill. He chose not to record specific treatment preferences today. The plan will be revisited yearly or after any serious illness. [S]
